analysis.one_liner: Sets written tests for when a worker can legally be treated as an independent contractor rather than an employee for federal taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 19, 1995 with 15 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law clear conditions under which a business and a worker can agree to treat the worker as an independent contractor instead of an employee for federal employment taxes. A worker would count as a contractor only with a written agreement meeting at least one of four tests, such as being able to make a profit or loss, running a separate place of business, serving multiple clients, or working purely on commission. It would also replace the older IRS 'safe harbor' rules with a revised version, raise penalties on companies that fail to send contractors their 1099 forms, and direct the Treasury Department to propose further criteria that give taxpayers 'maximum latitude' in deciding employment status.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that use independent contractors gain the most: a written qualified agreement plus a 'reasonable basis' safe harbor would give them certainty that the IRS cannot reclassify their workers as employees and bill them years of back employment taxes. Workers who genuinely freelance gain a defined legal status and a written agreement spelling out both sides' obligations and the worker's own tax responsibilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses using independent contractors, and freelancers

how_it_helps.text: A worker is treated as a contractor, and the firm as not an employer, only with a written agreement and if at least one of four independence tests is met: the worker can realize a profit or loss, maintains a separate place of business with a significant investment in tools, offers services to the public and works for another client, or is paid entirely on commission with a separate place of business.

The bill replaces Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978 with a codified safe harbor: a business that consistently reported a worker as a non-employee has no employment tax liability unless it had no reasonable basis, with reasonable basis including prior IRS audits with no assessment, judicial precedent or rulings, and long-standing industry practice.

It raises the penalty on companies that fail to furnish correct 1099 statements for service payments from $50 to $75 (and from $100 to $125 in some cases), and requires 1099 payments to be listed on a separate line of tax returns, making contractor income harder to under-report.

It directs the Treasury Department, within 180 days, to propose legislation with objectively measurable criteria for determining employment status, with Congress stating its intent that those criteria allow taxpayers maximum latitude.

analysis.who_pays: Workers shifted from employee to contractor status bear the full payroll tax themselves instead of splitting it with an employer, lose employer-provided benefits, and lose unemployment insurance coverage tied to employee wages. Social Security and unemployment insurance programs see their payroll-tax base shrink where firms reclassify. The IRS gives up some ability to reclassify workers it believes are really employees, since failing the bill's tests cannot itself be used as evidence of employee status.
analysis.who_pays_short: Reclassified workers and payroll-tax funded programs

drawbacks.text: The bill requires only a written agreement and one of four tests, and states that failing the tests 'shall not be construed as indicating that an individual is an employee,' which makes it harder for the IRS to reclassify workers who in substance work like employees.

The Congress states its intent that Treasury's criteria 'allow taxpayers maximum latitude in determining employment status,' tilting the future rules toward businesses rather than toward workers seeking employee protections.

Where a firm converts employees to contractors, the employer saves its share of payroll taxes and the cost of benefits and unemployment insurance, while the worker takes on the full self-employment tax and loses coverage those taxes would have funded.

The industry-practice safe harbor is explicitly loosened: a practice followed by as little as 25 percent of an industry qualifies, and the Treasury Secretary must allow taxpayers maximum latitude in picking which 'industry' to compare against.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real value on the legitimate side of the problem: genuine freelancers and small businesses get written, predictable rules instead of an audit gamble, and the higher 1099 penalties improve reporting. But the trade runs mostly one way financially. Because an employer saves its share of payroll taxes and benefits costs whenever a worker is classified as a contractor, easier classification creates a standing incentive to push employees out of employee status, and the bill's 'maximum latitude' language and its rule that failing the tests is not evidence of employment make that pressure easier to act on. The worker-consent requirements and the penalty increases are real mitigations, but they do not offset the incentive.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 19, 1995 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when that Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Kim of California introduced the Independent Contractor Tax Fairness Act on January 19, 1995.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill never advanced again.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with no vote in either chamber.
Fifteen members cosponsored the bill: 13 Republicans and 2 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses with contractor-heavy workforces are better off: the older Section 530 safe harbor stayed in place unrevised, the higher 1099 penalties never arrived, and no new written-agreement requirements were imposed. Workers got neither the bill's clarity nor any added protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses keeping the existing contractor safe harbor

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship leaned Republican (13 of 15 cosponsors were Republicans, 2 Democrats), but no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no evidence of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: Businesses that use independent contractors (trucking, sales, real estate, consulting, staffing)
industries.note: The qualified-agreement regime and the 'reasonable basis' safe harbor (including industry practice) would shield firms from IRS reclassification and back employment taxes, and employer status ends for covered workers. The financial gain comes largely from avoiding the employer share of payroll taxes and benefits obligations, costs that shift to workers and to the payroll-tax funded programs.

Genuine freelancers would gain a defined status, a written agreement spelling out services and pay, and protection from surprise reclassification. But they remain responsible for the full self-employment tax and for their own benefits and retirement, since no employer contribution exists.

industries.industry: Social Security and unemployment insurance (payroll-tax funded programs)
industries.note: Every worker moved from employee to contractor status removes wages from the payroll-tax base that funds Social Security and unemployment insurance, and removes that worker's unemployment coverage. The IRS also loses leverage to reclassify workers it believes are misclassified.
